item.title: Verifiable, private and decentralized orderflow processing with Automata Linux and TOOL
item.dc:creator: Automata Network
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Ethereum’s transaction supply chain currently relies on opaque intermediaries that raise concerns around privacy, neutrality, and centralization. TOOL (Trustless Orderflow Operations Layer) replaces this with a decentralized peer-to-peer network where operators process orderflow inside Trusted Execution Environments, providing transaction confidentiality as well as efficient and neutral execution environment. Through a collaboration with Automata Linux, TOOL achieves end-to-end verifiability: every node’s software state is cryptographically bound to its hardware identity, continuously attested, and anchored onchain, so the network can prove shared execution logic is correct without exposing operators’ private strategies. The result is a coordination layer where competition happens on common ground, backed by proofs rather than trust.

Ethereum blocks don’t appear out of nowhere; they’re the result of a complex supply chain with specialized entities responsible for transaction processing, before they’re packed into blocks that are sent to the Validators.

However, transactions often contain sensitive information, such as DeFi trades, loan liquidations, CEX deposits, and so on. Their execution results are also uncertain, until the block is signed by the Ethereum Validator.

At its core, orderflow is processed by operators that run proprietary algorithms. Yet, despite this opacity, these operators must coordinate with one another to produce valid execution outcomes.

This raises a lot of concerns: What if some of the intermediaries have too much control over transaction execution? How do they handle privacy? How transparent are they? Do they use 3rd party services that can abuse the insights from the transactions’ contents?

TOOL, which stands for Trustless Orderflow Operations Layer, developed by NuConstruct, solves all of these problems.It introduces a decentralized and permissionless peer-to-peer network where operators process orderflow inside Trusted Execution Environments. Instead of relying on centralized coordination or opaque intermediaries, participants run TOOL nodes that handle orderflow privately, generate commitments with execution results visible to other operators in the network, and achieve consensus on which commitments are going to be included in the block.

TOOL targets three properties simultaneously: privacy, neutrality, and efficiency. Orderflow remains confidential within TEEs. No actor can influence execution outcomes. Coordination is streamlined to reduce latency, enabling faster execution cycles and better composability to minimize the number of stale transactions.

Achieving end-to-end logic verifiability with Automata Linux

Simply running code inside a TEE only ensures isolation from the outside world. It does not ensure that the code itself is correct. If a node runs modified logic, leaks orderflow, or deviates from protocol rules, the system has no inherent way to detect it.

Automata Linux establishes an end-to-end verifiable pipeline from code to hardware. The goal is not simply to attest that a machine is secure, but to cryptographically bind the software state to the hardware identity throughout its entire lifecycle.

The process begins pre-deployment with atakit, a developer CLI that defines the workload as a fixed reference. It generates a SHA-256 fingerprint across all artifacts, including Docker containers, binaries, and configurations, creating a canonical representation of the system. Even a single-bit deviation invalidates future attestations.

This reference is then deployed onto an Automata Linux CVM base image, a reproducible environment built for confidential computing. Unlike standard cloud images, Automata Linux normalizes variables like timestamps and metadata to ensure the image is strictly deterministic and can be recreated exactly from source.

At runtime, the CVM Agent binds the application to the hardware. It measures the workload (including the TOOL container) and extends these values into the CPU’s attestation registers. This produces a report proving both the machine’s TEE authenticity and the integrity of the running code.

Finally, this attestation is anchored onchain via the CVM Registry. Through verifier contracts, reports are validated and recorded with a defined time-to-live (TTL). This requires machines to provide periodic re-attestation to remain trusted; if a machine fails to update its proof or is compromised, its identity is revoked.

Verification without the overhead

Historically, the barrier to entry for confidential computing has been prohibitively high. Leveraging TEEs required developers to navigate low-level hardware primitives and complex cryptographic attestation logic. This often led to fragmented, custom solutions and copious engineering hours.

Automata Linux upends this by providing a standardized, turnkey environment. By abstracting the complexities of the underlying hardware into a reproducible Linux stack, it allows teams to inherit a robust, verifiable foundation out of the box. What’s key is allowing developers to focus entirely on their core logic rather than the intricacies of attestation registries. By providing these capabilities as a ready-to-use layer, Automata Linux ensures that protocols can achieve end-to-end verifiability without the need to build the entire security stack from scratch.

Defining the boundary of trust

The TOOL container, which defines how orderflow is processed, is measured, attested, and verifiable. The operator containers, which define how value is extracted, remain private and unmeasured. This allows Searchers to retain full control over their strategies without exposing them, while the network can still verify that the shared execution layer is correct and the processing environment is safely isolated.

Maintaining this guarantee requires careful handling of updates and operations. Systems must evolve, but changes cannot be invisible. With Automata Linux, updates to workloads trigger re-measurement and new attestation proofs. The system effectively enforces continuous verification.

What emerges from this collaboration is a new model for coordination in credibly neutral decentralized systems, where the participants can safely compete for the best transaction execution on common ground.

We are entering an era where coordination no longer requires a leap of faith, but is instead established by the complementary mix of hardware and cryptographical proofs.

item.title: Agentic execution as a system: From thought to trade with XATA
item.dc:creator: Automata Network
item.content:encoded:
XATA is the agentic execution layer for onchain perpetuals. Turn ideas into live positions, now across Hyperliquid, including trade.xyz, Felix, and Ventuals, as well as Aster, and Lighter.

Most trading infrastructure is designed around the rigid structure of orders. These tools require you to pick a market, choose a venue, and manually set parameters, assuming that expressing a view is a simple task. In reality, trading begins long before an order is placed.

A trade usually starts as a belief or a specific condition. You might see funding turning negative across venues or realize a position needs to be hedged. When a signal fires, the priority is the market itself, not the menu of a terminal. What follows is a sequence: checking venues, deciding where to execute, structuring the position, and managing it over time.

As onchain perpetual markets have expanded, that sequence has become more complex. Liquidity is distributed across venues such as Hyperliquid, Aster, and Lighter, and execution quality depends on where and how trades are placed. Acting on a single idea can involve multiple systems, even for relatively simple strategies.

XATA closes this gap. It provides a unified execution layer across onchain perpetual venues, allowing both humans and automated systems to express a trading idea once and execute it across markets. What would normally require switching interfaces or writing custom logic becomes a single, consistent process.

XATA - Agentic execution layer for onchain perpetuals

Execution as a system

On XATA, AI plays a different role than typically assumed. The primary function is not prediction, but translation. It converts loosely defined intent, such as conditions, signals, or strategies, into structured, executable actions. It monitors those conditions continuously and triggers execution when they are met, reducing the need for manual coordination.

User: “I’m seeing a spike in AI token sentiment, but recent liquidations on Hyperliquid pushed $AI below Aster spot. I want to go long the widest spread and hedge if Lighter funding stays above 0.05% for over an hour.”

  • Synthesis: XATA scans real-time data across Hyperliquid, Aster, and Lighter to validate conditions.
  • Strategy Mapping: It identifies the widest spread between Hyperliquid and Aster and structures a delta-neutral position for mean reversion.
  • Execution: Once confirmed, the system routes the trade through low-latency paths, opening the long on Hyperliquid and coordinating the hedge on Lighter.

Liquidity is distributed, and the quality of an outcome depends on where and how trades are placed. XATA provides unified access to these venues, allowing both humans and agents to express an idea once and see it realized across markets without rebuilding workflows for every specific venue.

Engineered for agents

This system extends naturally to agents.

Agents plugging into XATA’s API inherit a professional-grade execution stack without having to build and maintain direct integrations with every individual DEX, while providing consistent access to liquidity and execution.

The infrastructure is defined by three core pillars:

  • Hardware-isolated security: Master keys are secured inside Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), and never exposed to agents. Instead, agents operate through restricted APIs scoped strictly to trading operations. Funds remain under hardware-level protection while execution is delegated.
  • Multi-venue execution: XATA maintains optimized, low-latency connections across venues including Hyperliquid, Aster, and Lighter. Agents access distributed liquidity through a unified interface, without managing venue-specific environments.
  • Intent-to-execution pipeline: The path from signal to execution is compressed. By reducing hops and minimizing latency, XATA ensures faster fills in markets where milliseconds matter. When the market moves, the pipeline determines the outcome.

Built for humans

Agents operate through APIs, but humans operate through thought.

This is the role of XATA Copilot, an interactive chat interface embedded directly into the trading UI. Unsure of how to structure a multi-venue trailing stop? Ask Copilot. Want to analyze market signals before committing capital? Copilot walks you through the data.

Beyond guidance, Copilot can analyze signals, structure trades, and trigger execution directly from your chat prompts. It translates human intent into structured execution in the same way the system does for agents. Agents use APIs. Humans use interfaces. Copilot ensures both operate on the same execution system.

XATA for the next turn of agentic trading

We are moving towards a hybrid model of finance. In this world, human judgment defines the intent, and machine intelligence handles the execution. Instead of navigating between venues and manually coordinating actions, users interact with a system that treats execution as an intelligent process. Traders and AI agents define what should happen, and systems ensure that it happens consistently across markets.

The abstraction of the order is no longer sufficient for how trading actually happens. What matters now is how ideas take shape in markets without breaking the flow between thinking and trading. And that’s XATA.

item.title: Hardening Machine Intelligence: Story Adopts Automata’s DCAP for Hardware-Anchored IP
item.dc:creator: Automata Network
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Story adopts Automata’s DCAP Attestation to operationalize hardware trust for the agentic IP economy. By leveraging the DCAP Dashboard to automate collateral management, Story ensures its Confidential Data Rails (CDR) and autonomous AI workloads are anchored in verifiable hardware without manual upkeep or operational downtime. This sets a new benchmark for verifiable machine intelligence.

Story is building AI-native infrastructure for the $80 trillion IP asset class, transforming intellectual property into machine-readable, programmable assets ready for autonomous workflows. As this ecosystem scales, much of the heavy computation, such as fine-tuning AI models on licensed data or processing complex revenue-sharing trees, requires Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) to handle off-chain workloads that exceed onchain capacity.

The integrity of hardware-isolated enclaves depends on remote attestation. Specifically, Intel DCAP allows a TEE to prove to an external party that it is genuine hardware running the correct, untampered code. Automata’s DCAP Attestation is the industry standard for verifying hardware integrity onchain, with built-in zkVM integrations including Risc Zero, Succinct and Brevis. This allows high-fidelity hardware trust to become practical for autonomous workflows.

Powering Confidential Data Rails (CDR)

The integration of DCAP Attestation is significant for Story’s Confidential Data Rails (CDR), its cryptographic framework that turns encrypted data into programmable onchain building blocks. CDR allows IP owners to define exactly when, where, and how sensitive data, ranging from AI training sets to genomic vaults, is unlocked.

This is achieved through a decentralized TEE network. While the smart contract verifies the programmatic rules, TEEs perform the sensitive work of decrypting keys through threshold decryption. By securing these rails with Automata’s DCAP framework, Story ensures that private data remains portable yet strictly permissioned. Rules are physically enforced by attested silicon for tamper-proof operations.

From silicon to settlement

And yet managing attestation infrastructure for underlying TEE infrastructure is notoriously complex. Remote attestation relies on a series of signed certificates and security status updates provided by the hardware manufacturer. These files must be constantly synchronized and updated; if they expire or rotate without being refreshed, hardware verification fails.

For a production-grade network like Story, manual management of these trust chains is not a scalable solution. Automata has successfully deployed its DCAP Attestation and onchain PCCS contracts to Story Mainnet and Story Aeneid Testnet. While the PCCS contract serves as a decentralized repository for hardware credentials, DCAP Dashboard provides the unified interface to:

  • Automate collateral upserts: Instead of manual certificate management, the dashboard handles the recurring task of fetching and updating Intel DCAP collaterals directly to the PCCS contracts on Story.
  • Ensure continuous validity: It automates the refresh cycle of Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) to prevent silent failures that often plague hardware-based systems.
  • Bridge the trust gap: By hosting its own decentralized PCCS, Story replaces the need for proprietary caching services with a native, onchain verifier suite. This removes the single point of failure inherent in solely manufacturer-hosted servers.

Anchoring the agentic economy

An agent-driven IP economy is only as resilient as the hardware it inhabits. For Story, DCAP Attestation provides the technical audit necessary to link autonomous AI workloads to the physical integrity of secure enclaves. Further, indexing these attestations on the Automata Attestation Explorer transforms hardware state into a public trust input and allows the industry to reason about AI security in a transparent manner.

When AI model inputs and licensing outputs are processed within a verified hardware perimeter, the global AI-IP stack becomes a closed loop of cryptographic trust. With Automata adding support for Story with DCAP Attestation, Story establishes the physical state of its compute environment as a transparent and auditable truth on par with the blockchain itself.

item.title: Rounding up 2025 with Automata
item.dc:creator: Automata Network
item.content:encoded:
​​Every year in Web3 feels fast. Some years, however, feel formative. 2025 was one of those years, where compute demand accelerated at a rapid pace, with AI as a major driver. As complex offchain systems mature and are increasingly being integrated with the onchain world, smart contracts require more visibility into the execution itself, instead of just trusting the result.

At Automata, this belief has guided our work since the beginning. Over the past year, it became increasingly shared across our ecosystem. Verifiable machines are expanding into different Web3 verticals as more applications adopt secure hardware, with attestations as the anchor of trust for provable execution. Looking back on our top accomplishments, we’re encouraged by the steady momentum we’ve achieved as we move towards a new age for agents and decentralized systems.

Furthering the roadmap for Ethereum

One of the strongest signals is secure hardware being recognized within Ethereum’s long-term direction. In the shift towards privacy and decentralization for the broader ecosystem, TEEs offer a practical primitive for offchain execution with confidentiality and integrity guarantees.

And we’re now seeing this in action:

  • 1RPC: As Ethereum shifts towards prioritizing user-level privacy, Automata’s zero-tracking relay was highlighted by Vitalik Buterin in his privacy roadmap. TEE-based RPC privacy provides onchain verifiable guarantees that users’ metadata are protected against harvesting. To date, 1RPC has protected over 49 billion relays across 64 networks.
  • Secure L2s with fast finality: More rollups are reaching Stage 1 decentralization, and the next challenge involves ​​achieving fast withdrawal times without compromising security guarantees. A hybrid OP + ZK + TEE proof system was proposed by Vitalik Buterin to provide a 2-of-3 guarantee that state transitions are valid while removing the potential for single points of failure. With adoption from the likes of Scroll and Linea, Automata’s Multi-Prover AVS offers secondary verification rollups with a decentralized network of TEE-based provers without significant latency or cost overhead.

Our efforts towards minimizing UX failures on Ethereum include open-sourcing the UniFi TDX Prover alongside Puffer Finance. As a concrete example of how TEEs can deliver hardware-backed fast finality, UniFi has achieved real-time proving with sub-10ms attestation of blocks while introducing hardware redundancy through multiple TEE vendors (Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP).

The machine trust layer for the agentic economy and beyond

Agents can now make independent financial decisions, but what remains unresolved is trust. How does a counterparty or user verify that the agent is genuine and behaving as expected within defined constraints?

This year, ERC-8004 has established a standardized framework for an agent’s reputation to be deployable and verifiable onchain, an immutable record that can be recorded, retrieved, and audited. With TEE attestations as one of the three recognized trust models, it offers hardware-level guarantees that the agentic code is genuine and execution is private.

To support this emerging registry and continue our mission to bring TEEs onchain, Automata continued to expand what is now the most complete stack for hardware-attested agents:

  • DCAP Attestation: Publishing of our Trail of Bits audit for the DCAP Attestation library and the release of v1.1 that transitions the library into a monorepo and operational improvements that are built for onchain agents.
  • DCAP Dashboard: Removing operational burden of maintaining the trust chain for Intel SGX and TDX by automating collateral upkeep and quote management in attestation workflows.
  • Attestation SDKs: Release of the zk verifier for AWS Nitro Enclaves to complete Automata’s suite of production-ready attestation SDKs alongside Intel SGX, Intel TDX, and AMD SEV-SNP. Developers can build verifiably trusted applications without the underlying complexity of TEE attestation.
  • Attestation explorer: All TEE attestations from the DCAP verifier contract are publicly verifiable across 24+ mainnets and testnets, with over 790,000 attestations published to date. As the agentic economy matures, the explorer serves as a map to link agents to their hardware identity and the integrity of code being executed.

Beyond agents, onchain attestations serve as the bridge between the digital and physical world, with trusted machine workloads forming a new primitive on Ethereum. Automata’s DCAP Attestation stack has become one of the most widely used building blocks for verifiable hardware execution across Web3, supporting integrations with leading projects like Flashtestations by Flashbots, Jovay Network by Ant Digital, Secret Network, t1 Protocol, NuConstruct, and many more.

Strengthening the ZK + TEE synergy

ZK is better with TEEs, and so are TEEs with ZK. Throughout 2025, we leaned further into a defense-in-depth philosophy that combines both mathematical guarantees and hardware trust.

Automata has been working closely with the top ZK-based projects to build on this synergy:

  • OP Succinct Lite: Automata’s OP stack rollup adopted single-step ZK fault proofs to reduce finality times to 1 day, providing fast onchain acceptance for validating agentic actions.
  • Private proving for Brevis’ Pico Prism: TEEs provide confidential execution environments to protect sensitive witness data from proving operators, while being verifiable with Automata’s DCAP verification.
  • Adding Brevis Pico to DCAP Attestation v1.1: Increasing prover diversity alongside other guest programs like Risc Zero Boundless and Succinct SP1 for developers to choose the best proving system that matches their demands. Proving programs collapse costly TEE verification checks onchain and make continuous validation of offchain workloads practical.

Commitment to trustlessness and education

Supply chain attacks have plagued the industry and resulted in multiple preventable attacks, usually the result of malicious code being introduced in the gap between source code and deployed binaries.

In line with the Trustless Manifesto, Automata removes trusted intermediaries from the deployed binaries by making verification of software provenance viable onchain. Proof of Build involves verifying an SLSA attestation using Sigstore in zkVMs before posting the build onchain.

As we continue shipping strong tooling for developers to build TEE-based implementations, we believe that education plays a part in flattening the learning curve. Alongside industry-leading projects, we are heartened to see the collaborative nature as we launched the TEE Wiki, an open-source knowledge hub for anyone to gain a quick start in learning TEEs. (Contributions are open as we make this a public good for anyone to build and learn about TEEs.)

We’ve also shared these ideas globally, with headline talks at ETHDenver, EthCC and ETHTaipei. We are encouraged to see the growing interest in TEEs and how they can be integrated into future workloads.

All other resources from Automata on TEEs can be accessed in our Awesome repository.

Building a demonstrably honest future

A great deal has shifted since Automata began our journey. And yet in many ways, we are still at the beginning.

2025 has made it clear how fast the TEE landscape can grow, with much more remaining to be built. Provable workloads become a fundamental primitive to make computations real and trusted. Working together with our community and fellow builders across the ecosystem has given us a stronger conviction that verifiable machines are the future for Ethereum, agents, and decentralized systems.

Through all of this, our commitment remains unchanged: to provide the tooling required to establish machine trust in a trustless environment. Here’s to a great 2026.

item.title: Proof of Build: Verifiable software provenance onchain
item.dc:creator: Automata Network
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Aligned with the Trustless Manifesto, Automata’s Proof of Build enforces verifiable software provenance onchain. Proof of Build verifies SLSA + Sigstore bundle inside a zkVM (RISC Zero Boundless, Succinct SP1, or Brevis Pico), and publishes a lightweight proof for smart contracts to validate that deployed binaries match a specific source commit and builder identity.

Trustless systems, as outlined in the Trustless Manifesto, replace trust with enforced verification.

Our industry relies on a social assumption: if a project is open-source, we assume the deployed binary is a faithful reproduction of that source. Between the human-readable Solidity or Rust code on GitHub and the machine-readable executable code on Ethereum, there is a disconnect between “what we see” (source code) and “what we run” (build output). The system is structurally fragile because correctness is dependent on the goodwill of intermediaries.

Automata’s Proof of Build addresses this air gap.

Open-source doesn’t guarantee correct deployment

Making provenance verification computationally viable onchain enables new enforcement patterns in Web3. There are a number of scenarios where Proof of Build has immediate utility in deployment pipelines:

In late 2023, a malicious version of the Ledger Connect Kit was injected into dApps. A malicious actor compromised the NPM account of a developer at Ledger, having injected a “wallet drainer” into the connect-kit library.

  • With Proof of Build: The ZK proof would have checked the build against the official GitHub repository’s hash. The malicious library, having been injected after the source code stage or outside the verified pipeline, would fail to generate a valid proof. The smart contract or client would simply reject it.

DAOs vote on a description of code, but trust a multisig to deploy the matching bytecode. Voters technically have no guarantee that multisig signers are deploying the exact proposal they approved.

  • With Proof of Build: The governance contract can enforce that the upgrade transaction must carry a proof linking the new bytecode to the specific git commit voted upon. The multisig signers become mere couriers; they cannot swap the code for a malicious version without invalidating the proof.

A standard for software provenance

As it stands, the broader software industry has converged on two complementary frameworks: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) and Sigstore. Together, they produce an SLSA provenance file embedded within a Sigstore bundle, a canonical, industry-standard representation of software provenance: Did the expected builder identity produce this specific artifact from this specific source commit, and can we prove the signature existed at that time?

Validating this answer onchain is where our current architecture breaks down. To faithfully verify a Sigstore bundle directly on a general-purpose chain (e.g. EVM), a verifier must do one of several things: parse X.509 Certificates that requires traversing complex certificate chains and ASN.1 structures; verify transparency logs to calculate Merkle path inclusion proofs to ensure the signature was publicly logged; perform gas-heavy crypto operations such as verifying signatures (often ECDSA P-256 or P-384) that may not have cheap precompiles on the target blockchain.

Solving the onchain complexity

If we want smart contracts and decentralized systems to directly consume provenance as a trust input, we need a way that:

  • Is not economically and practically prohibitive
  • Expose only a small set of verified facts onchain
  • Avoid trusting a central verifier

Automata accomplishes this by using a zkVM (supporting RISC Zero Boundless, Succinct SP1, or Brevis Pico) to output a tiny, constant-sized proof that is cheap to verify onchain. This also allows for:

  • Verifiability without trust in a particular operator: Anyone can re-run the zkVM program and check that the onchain verifier circuit matches the published code/hash.
  • Composability across chains: A single proof can be generated once and verified on Ethereum, Optimism, and Arbitrum simultaneously.
  • Policy flexibility onchain: Smart contracts can enforce arbitrary logic over the verified journal. A contract can say: “I will only accept artifacts built from the ‘main’ branch of ‘uniswap/v4-core’.

Making verifiable provenance the trustless standard

Automata’s Proof of Build workflow proceeds in four distinct stages:

  1. Generation: The CI/CD pipeline builds the code and creates an SLSA provenance file, signing it via the Sigstore infrastructure.
  2. Ingestion (zkVM input): The zkVM guest program takes in this SLSA provenance bundle alongside the pinned Sigstore trust roots (Fulcio CA, TSA public keys), and optionally, an expected policy (e.g., allowed build digests, subjects and issuers.).
  3. Execution: Inside the zero-knowledge environment, the guest program performs the heavy lifting. It checks that the signature bundle is valid, that the certificate chain is correct, that the timestamp or transparency proof is present, and that the identity and source information satisfy the expected policy. If all checks pass, it emits a minimal journal containing only the verified fields (e.g., artifact digest, repo, ref, builder identity, timestamp).
  4. Settlement: The zkVM produces a succinct proof that the provenance verification succeeded.

For technical specifications, visit: Automata Proof of Build explainer site.

item.title: Automata’s release of DCAP Attestation v1.1 for agentic systems
item.dc:creator: Automata Network
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Automata today maintains the most complete, production-ready verifier suite across Intel, AMD, and Nitro TEEs. DCAP Attestation v1.1, deployed on over twenty networks including Optimism, HyperEVM and World Chain, adds Pico zkVM support, Quote V5 verification, and fine-grained TCB Recovery controls, along with improvements to the Attestation Explorer. Together, these form the canonical foundation for ERC-8004 agents to anchor their identity in verifiable hardware.

We are excited to announce the v1.1 release of our comprehensive TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) verification stack. This release hardens our entire suite of tools; including our core DCAP Attestation verifier, our developer CLI which handles ZK attestation proofs and also interfaces with Automata’s onchain PCCS for collateral verification, and the Attestation Explorer, which provides a unified interface for anyone to explore and verify onchain attestations.

Across L2s, AI-native platforms, and now agentic systems, developers are reaching for TEEs as a foundation for trust. And yet, remote attestation has historically been hard to operationalize. DCAP Attestation reduces that opacity by placing collaterals, evaluation pathways, and verification logic onto a transparent, public ledger. This has made it one of the most widely adopted open-source verifier stack for projects building real systems today, including Flashtestations by the Flashbots team, Jovay Network by Ant Digital, Espresso, Phala Network, Secret Network, Oasis Network, t1 protocol, and Stoffel MPC, among others.

The release of DCAP Attestation v1.1 builds directly on this trajectory and extends the utility of secure hardware into the agent-driven systems beginning to define the next phase of our industry.

DCAP Attestation is good for ERC-8004

v1.1 completes our transition to a public monorepo, giving developers one authoritative repository for all DCAP Attestation components, versioning, and tooling. While the full release includes many operational improvements, the features below more directly address the requirements of trustless onchain agents as demonstrated by ERC-8004:

Pico zkVM for SNARK attestation

TEE quote verification is computationally heavy with raw quotes that contain detailed hardware state. In addition to native onchain verification, DCAP Attestation enables SNARK-based attestation to shrink both the computation and the gas footprint. The release of v1.1 adds support for Pico by Brevis to its roster of guest programs including Risc Zero and Succinct, which also reflects a broader principle in proving diversity.

With v1.1, DCAP Attestation continues to treat ZK programs as a modular component, allowing teams to choose that which best matches their constraints while maintaining a consistent attestation interface.

Support for Quote V5 verification

Remote attestation is evolving rapidly as Intel TDX gains traction for cloud-based enclave workloads. We have therefore fully implemented verification for Quote V5, Intel’s latest attestation format, which unifies SGX quote bodies, TDX 1.0 reports, and next-generation TDX 1.5 reports under a single, more future-proof structure.

v1.1 also updates the onchain output format to clearly differentiate between these distinct report types. This ensures long-term compatibility for teams working across diverse environments as agents are verified cleanly today whether across SGX or TDX deployments.

Advanced TCB Recovery modes

We’ve introduced the AutomataTcbEvalDao contract so developers can now explicitly choose which TCB Evaluation Data Number to verify against. Verification can be anchored to an exact Intel TCB Recovery event, which allows developers to codify their own trust assumptions.

Agents can enforce stricter security for sensitive workloads, preserve broad compatibility during new advisory periods, or guarantee deterministic behavior; by pinning a TCB number, a multi-operator agentic network (like an AVS or MPC) can ensure all nodes are using the exact same ruleset. Attestation is no longer a binary validity check but becomes aligned with the precise security posture an agent requires.

Gas-efficient attestations via EIP-7951

DCAP Attestation v1.1 also integrates support for the EIP-7951 precompile, anticipating Ethereum’s Fusaka upgrade. This slashes the gas cost of ECDSA signature verification from ~330,000 to just 6,000 gas*, reducing the total onchain verification cost by nearly 1 million gas. TEE-based validation becomes economically viable at scale, enabling agents to provide continuous proof of their integrity.

*As evidenced on Sepolia and Hoodi testnets

Mapping agentic trust pathways

Automata’s attestation explorer currently surfaces onchain attestations, raw quote metadata, and outputs from the DCAP verifier contract. As TEEs become foundational infrastructure for agent networks, several improvements follow naturally from v1.1 and from the direction of the ecosystem.

First, as the TEE landscape diversifies, the attestation explorer becomes a canonical map of the trust infrastructure itself, showing where verifier contracts are deployed and annotating each attestation with the exact verifier path used. This fits naturally with Automata’s work today; alongside DCAP Attestation, we already maintain one of the most complete sets of verifier contracts across AMD SEV-SNP and AWS Nitro.

Second, to provide a clear map of attestation entry points, revealing the systems agents actively rely on. By cross-referencing an agent’s public registry ID with its raw, cryptographic TEE attestation, the explorer directly links an agent’s identity to its provable hardware state. Security assumptions can be reasoned in a transparent manner. We’re actively looking to integrate with several explorer dashboards within the ERC-8004 landscape, and aim to share more in the upcoming weeks.

A brand new (agentic) world

ERC-8004 provides the blueprint for the trustless agent economy. And DCAP Attestation v1.1 arrives at a moment when the trust layer for agents is finally taking shape. Whereas the former defines the high-level foundation for agents — how they identify themselves, are discovered, and build trust — Automata’s work anchors that foundation by grounding those identities in verifiable hardware.

As more workloads migrate into TEEs and more agents operate across heterogeneous environments, the coherence of this stack matters. v1.1 strengthens that coherence. With DCAP Attestation v1.1, we are no longer just attesting to hardware. We are providing the foundational trust for a shiny, new agent economy.

item.title: How Automata and Cantina enable verifiable AI agents for ERC-8004
item.dc:creator: Automata Network
item.content:encoded:
The age of autonomous AI agents is here, but it brings a fundamental challenge. As agents begin to manage assets and execute complex tasks onchain, the need to move beyond opaque, black-box operations has never been more urgent.

This high-stakes environment demands a new trust primitive. Ethereum standards like ERC-8004 call for agents to build a verifiable, onchain reputation. Automata is excited to be collaborating with Cantina to make this a practical reality, delivering the hardware-attested foundation for this new agentic economy.

Hardware-verified AI agents

At the heart of this new economy is the TEE-attested agent.

A TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) is a secure area inside a processor. A TEE-attested agent is an AI agent that uses this secure hardware to cryptographically prove its integrity. It allows the agent to demonstrate to a smart contract, or any other party, that it is running the correct, unmodified code and that its private data and models are secure.

This process is called remote attestation. It is the core mechanism that allows a smart contract to cryptographically trust a remote AI agent without having to trust its human owner.

This is precisely what ERC-8004 formalizes. The standard defines TEE attestation as the cryptographic proof model, enabling agents to register, validate, and build reputation based on hardware-level guarantees.

ERC-8004 with Automata

Automata provides a complete, two-part solution that makes onchain attestation practical, cost-effective, and continuous for agentic workloads.

Automata DCAP Dashboard: This is a complete management system that automates the entire collateral lifecycle for Intel SGX/TDX. It eliminates the risk of silent failures by managing the four key pillars of attestation:

  • Anchor: Publishes all DCAP collateral onchain, creating a single, publicly auditable source of truth.
  • Maintain: Provides 24/7, automated upkeep by tracking Intel’s TCB changes and certificate expirations, pushing updates onchain to keep attestations valid.
  • Verify: Allows developers to submit quotes to validate an enclave’s integrity or use the dashboard to test and monitor attestation status.
  • Audit: Includes a built-in activity log that records every collateral update and attestation event for full transparency.

Broad-Support Attestation SDKs: Beyond Intel, Automata provides a suite of SDKs with broad support for all major TEE families, including AMD SEV-SNP and AWS Nitro, ensuring verifiable integrity for all TEE-based agents.

The future of verifiable AI

Automata is working together with Cantina to secure the complete development stack:

  • Automata provides verifiable, hardware-grade trust for AI agents
  • Cantina provides the essential tooling and security for agentic applications built on that infrastructure

To accelerate the development of secure, TEE-attested agents, projects building within the Automata ecosystem will receive streamlined access to Cantina’s security platform. This includes preferential pricing on solutions and complimentary bug bounty programs to secure their entire application stack.

Reach out here: https://cantina.xyz/introduction/automata-cantina

item.title: On verifiable TEEs and ERC-8004: Hardware-attested agents
item.dc:creator: Automata Network
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: ERC-8004 formalizes trust between agents through feedback, validation, and hardware-based attestation. Automata’s attestation SDKs use proving systems powered by Risc Zero and Succinct, while the DCAP Dashboard maintains onchain validity. Together, they enable efficient, verifiable TEEs and a path towards fully hardware-attested agents.

Of the large volume of responses presented to the challenges of the agentic age, most tend to focus on the establishment of trust in an otherwise trustless environment, and fittingly so. The entire future of our civilization may well depend on how it turns out: Will our digital overlords be fettered to digital chains, or are we predestined to our fate as pets in an AI-dominated world? The goal of this post will explore the reality of using verifiable TEEs (Trusted Execution Environments) today to get the benefits of an agentic economy without the downsides.

For many applications, we don’t want to merely prove that the model is being executed correctly, but also that it was the intended model that ran. A TEE, whether Intel SGX, Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, or AWS Nitro, acts as a verifiable hardware vault for code execution. It guarantees three properties crucial for agents:

  • Confidentiality: Data and model weights inside the enclave cannot be read by the host OS, hypervisor, or cloud provider.
  • Integrity: Code cannot be modified or inspected during runtime.
  • Remote Attestation: Enclave produces a signed report, that is, an attestation, proving that it’s running unmodified code on genuine hardware.

TEE Attestation as a trust model

ERC-8004 defines three pluggable trust models: feedback, inference validation, and TEE attestation, each corresponding to: social proof, economic proof and cryptographic proof. TEE attestation anchors trust at the infrastructure layer. Other agents can verify the attestation proof (e.g., DCAP quote or TDX proof) before trusting the output.

This framework forms a neutral, machine-verifiable chain of trust:

  • Hardware attestation (TEE) ensures the code is genuine
  • ERC-8004 ensures the attestation is recorded and retrievable
  • and subsequent interactions build a verifiable reputation around these guarantees.

Completing the TEE stack for agents

TEE attestation, however, involves complex cryptography and vendor-specific dependencies

that are difficult to verify onchain. The challenges are twofold: (a) High gas cost: Verifying a full Intel TDX or SGX quote in Solidity can consume several million gas; and (b) High maintenance complexity: Intel’s attestation collaterals (TCB, PCK, FMSPC) expire every month, and require regular synchronization to keep verification valid.

Without practical tooling, the concept of TEE-attested agents remains aspirational. Our present-day efforts to improve the state of hardware verifiability span a suite of attestation SDKs, including for Intel SGX, Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, and AWS Nitro. With the release of the zk verifier for AWS Nitro Enclaves, Automata completes support for all major TEE families. Proving programs powered by Risc Zero and Succinct collapse costly attestation checks into a single zk proof, making continuous validation practical within agent frameworks like ERC-8004.

Alongside our open-source attestation SDKs, Automata’s DCAP Dashboard also automates the collateral upkeep and quote management required for Intel SGX and TDX attestations. These verification flows are already in production: over 700,000 agent transactions have been verified on Magic Newton using DCAP Attestation, showing how standardized attestation can extend trust from human users to autonomous agents.

ERC-8004: Machine-verifiable chain of trust

TEE attestation as a first-class trust model, as expounded by ERC-8004, is designed to accommodate agents that prove their integrity through hardware-based attestation, and therefore register, validate, and advertise proofs of trusted execution. Open-sourcing our SDKs was a necessary precondition, and we’re excited to see the community build agentic applications with security assurances that are intelligible and verifiable by the user.

We may never entirely avoid having agentic workflows, or agents, that are deeply embedded in all aspects of our (personal and collective) lives, and indeed we should not. The question, as compared to the past trappings of a centralized world, is not if we can do better, but by how much.
